meta.tagline: France's oldest city — and its most misunderstood

pills: Go to the fish market before 10:00

overview.intro: Marseille is 2,600 years old, founded by Greek sailors, and has spent most of that time being underestimated. Paris looks down on it. Tourists skip it. Marseillais don't care. The Vieux-Port has been the city's beating heart since the Greeks arrived around 600 BC. The Calanques are some of the most dramatic coastline in Europe. The fish market runs every morning, fishermen selling from the same boats, the same way. MuCEM is one of the best-designed museums on the continent. None of this is secret. The secret is that the city works — loud, proud, and completely itself.

local_word.definition: What every Marseillais calls Notre-Dame de la Garde — the basilica that watches over the city from the highest hill. Ships leaving the port looked up at her. Ships returning looked up at her. She's on every sailor's ex-voto hung inside. 'La Bonne Mère' means 'the good mother'. The name says everything about how this city relates to the sea and to faith. Free entry. Go at dusk.

rules.title: The fish market is over by 10:00
rules.description: Every morning, fishermen sell the night's catch directly from their boats along the Quai des Belges at the Vieux-Port. This is one of the last markets of its kind in Europe — no middlemen, no wholesalers. By 10:00 it's finished. By 11:00 the quay is empty. Go at 08:00, before the restaurants arrive to buy. Free to walk through. Nothing to buy unless you have a kitchen.

rules.title: Bouillabaisse has a charter — and it matters
rules.description: The real bouillabaisse uses specific Mediterranean rockfish — rascasse, grondin, Saint-Pierre — and follows the Bouillabaisse Charter that Marseille restaurants sign. It is expensive, served in two courses, and takes hours. The €20 tourist-menu version is a different dish. Eat it once, at a restaurant that has signed the charter, and understand what the fuss is about. This is where it was invented.

rules.title: Marseille is not a city you rush
rules.description: The Calanques require planning — in summer, access to some coves is restricted due to fire risk and must be booked online. MuCEM has queues by midday; go early or late. Notre-Dame de la Garde is a 30-minute uphill walk from the port, or bus 60 from Hôtel de Ville. Le Panier is best before 11:00, before the day-trippers arrive. Give yourself three days minimum.

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.sub: Single ticket €1.70 · 24h pass €5.20 · Le Vélo first 30 min free

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: May–Jun ideal · Jul–Aug hot and busy · Sep–Oct perfect · winter mild

quick_facts.label: Fish market
quick_facts.sub: Fishermen sell direct from boats · done by 10:00 · free to visit

tip.label: Free access — MuCEM without a ticket
tip.text: The MuCEM galleries are ticketed, but the outdoor walkways, rooftop terrace, and Fort Saint-Jean next door are completely free. The footbridge connecting MuCEM to Fort Saint-Jean costs nothing. Fort Saint-Jean itself — a 17th-century fortress with gardens and ramparts overlooking the Vieux-Port — is free. The MuCEM terrace offers some of the best views of the port and the sea in the city. First Sunday of every month: museum galleries also free.

overview.title: Welcome to Marseille

transport.intro: Marseille is a large, hilly city. The centre is walkable. The Calanques, beaches, and outer neighbourhoods need buses. The RTM network covers everything — use it.

items.title: Airport → City Centre
items.description: The Navette Marseille shuttle runs between the airport and Saint-Charles train station every 15–20 minutes, journey around 25 minutes, paid on board. From Saint-Charles, the metro and tram connect to the rest of the city. Taxis run on meter, significantly more expensive.

items.title: Metro — two lines, well placed
items.description: Line 1 runs east-west through the centre: Vieux-Port, Noailles, Castellane. Line 2 runs north-south: Saint-Charles, Joliette (for MuCEM), Rond-Point du Prado. Single ticket €1.70, valid 60 minutes on all RTM transport. 24-hour pass €5.20. Buy at machines in every station.

items.title: Buses — essential for the coast
items.description: Bus 60 to Notre-Dame de la Garde from Hôtel de Ville. Bus 83 along the Corniche — Vallon des Auffes, Prado beaches, Malmousque. Bus B1 from Castellane metro to Sormiou calanque. Same RTM ticket as the metro. The coastal route on bus 83 is one of the best urban bus rides in France.

items.title: Le Vélo — bikes across the centre
items.description: Over 100 stations, 1,000 bikes. First 30 minutes free with a subscription. Flat enough in the centre; the hills start immediately once you leave the port area. Useful for Vieux-Port to Le Panier, Cours Julien, or along the seafront to MuCEM.

items.title: Walking — the only way to know Le Panier
items.description: Vieux-Port to MuCEM: 10 minutes. Vieux-Port to Le Panier: 15 minutes uphill. Notre-Dame de la Garde: 30–40 minutes steep walk from the port, or bus 60. Le Panier's alleyways cannot be navigated any other way. Wear shoes you can walk in.

callout.label: Bus 83 — the Corniche route
callout.text: Bus 83 runs along the Corniche Kennedy — the coastal road that curves around the bay south of the Vieux-Port. On the left: sea, rocks, swimmers. On the right: Belle Époque villas, palm trees, the city above. Vallon des Auffes appears below a bridge — you'll miss it if you're not looking. Prado beaches at the end. Same RTM ticket. Sit on the left side of the bus.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Marseille's neighbourhoods are distinct. Proximity to the Vieux-Port is convenient but not always where the city actually lives.

local_word.definition: Marseille's oldest neighbourhood — built on the hill above the Vieux-Port, on the site of the original Greek settlement. The name means 'the basket'. Streets too narrow for cars, laundry between windows, cats on steps. Artists have been moving in for decades, which means galleries, murals, and gentrification exist side by side. Still the most atmospheric place to be based in the city.

items.name: Le Panier
items.description: The oldest part of the city, above the Vieux-Port. Narrow alleys, street art, the Vieille Charité — a 17th-century almshouse now used as a museum and exhibition space. Mornings are quiet; by 11:00 the day-trippers arrive. Best neighbourhood to be based in if you want to feel the city rather than just see it.

items.name: Vieux-Port / 1er arrondissement
items.description: Around the old harbour. Everything starts here. Fish market in the morning, aperitif terraces at sundown, the ferry to Château d'If from the quay. Central, expensive, and loud at night. Close to MuCEM, Le Panier, and the ferry terminal. Best for short stays.

items.name: Noailles / Notre-Dame du Mont
items.description: Noailles is Marseille's most multicultural neighbourhood — Algerian, Moroccan, Comorian, Armenian communities, all present since the city was a major port of arrival. The market spills across the streets: spices, olives, flatbread, cheap produce. Notre-Dame du Mont just above is where younger Marseillais actually go out. Cours Julien is at the edge — street art, organic market on Wednesdays.

items.name: Joliette / Euromed
items.description: The regenerated port district around MuCEM. New hotels, the Docks (a 19th-century warehouse turned offices and restaurants), and direct access to MuCEM and Fort Saint-Jean. Not yet a neighbourhood in the full sense — more infrastructure than community. Best if MuCEM and the port area are the priority.

items.name: Prado / 8ème arrondissement
items.description: South of the centre, along the coast. Access to the Prado beaches, Parc Borély, and the start of the Calanques road. More residential, more Marseillais, fewer tourists. Metro or bus to the centre. Best if the Calanques are the main reason to be there.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Marseille has 300 days of sun. The question is not whether to go but when to avoid the crowds.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Right Season
items.description: May and June are the best months. Temperatures around 20–25°C, the sea is warming up, the Calanques are fully accessible without summer fire restrictions, and the tourist crowds haven't arrived. The Vieux-Port morning market is at its most active. Prices for accommodation are 30–40% lower than August. Marseille in May is the version the city prefers for itself.

callout.label: Calanques access in summer — check before you go
callout.text: From mid-June to mid-September, access to some calanques (particularly Sugiton, Morgiou, and Marseilleveyre) is restricted on certain days due to fire risk. The restriction is communicated 48 hours in advance and changes daily depending on the Météo-France fire index. Check the Parc National des Calanques website or app the day before. Access is free but limited. Bus B1 from Castellane metro to Sormiou runs year-round.

items.subtitle: Spring · Warm, uncrowded, Calanques fully open

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot and Crowded
items.description: July and August: the entire south of France is here. Calanque access restricted on high fire-risk days. Vieux-Port restaurants double their prices. The city itself is still Marseille — beaches, pastis, late dinners — but it requires patience. If you go in summer, stay away from the Vieux-Port at dinner and eat inland. The neighbourhoods absorb the tourists; the port does not.

callout.label: L'Estaque — the village the crowds forget
callout.text: L'Estaque is a former fishing village 10 kilometres north of the centre, now absorbed into the city but still separate in feel. Cézanne and Braque painted here repeatedly — the light over the bay was the point. The village has a few restaurants, a small beach, and almost no tourists in summer because no guidebook sends anyone there. Bus 35 from Joliette. The chichi frégi — a local fried dough speciality — is sold from stands near the port.

items.subtitle: Summer · Peak season, manage accordingly

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Best-Kept Secret
items.description: September and October: the sea is at its warmest (22–24°C), the Calanques are fully open again, the crowds are gone, and the city returns to its own rhythm. Restaurant prices drop. Hotel availability opens. The light turns golden and lower. The Marseillais who left for August come back. This is the version of the city that residents actually prefer — and almost no visitor knows it.

callout.label: September swimming in the Calanques
callout.text: After a full summer of heating, the sea in September reaches its peak temperature. The Calanques trails are quiet — weekday mornings you can have Sugiton or En-Vau largely to yourself. The limestone turns a different colour in autumn light: warmer, more amber. Bring water (no sources on the trails), start early, and check fire restrictions even in September — they can persist into the first weeks of the month.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Warm sea, empty calanques, lower prices

items.label: Winter
items.name: Mild and Overlooked
items.description: Winter in Marseille is mild — rarely below 10°C, often 15°C and sunny. The Mistral wind can be sharp and sustained for days, but between the Mistrals the city is quietly beautiful. Museums have no queues. The fish market runs. The neighbourhood cafés fill with locals. Notre-Dame de la Garde on a clear winter morning, with the Alps visible to the north — this is not the Marseille that most tourists see.

callout.label: The Mistral — what it is and how to read it
callout.text: The Mistral is a cold, dry wind from the northwest that can blow at 70–90 km/h for three days at a time. It makes the sky exceptionally clear and the light sharp, but it makes outdoor dining and coastal walking unpleasant. Locals know: when the Mistral blows, go to Le Panier (sheltered by the hill), eat indoors, and wait. It stops as suddenly as it starts. The day after a Mistral, Marseille looks like it was just cleaned.

items.subtitle: Winter · 15°C, empty, fully local

monthly_highlights.text: Fête du Panier: the oldest quarter celebrates for two days with street concerts and open workshops.
Peak Calanques season: cove access can be restricted — plan early hours or a boat; the city beaches are in full swing.
The secret season: the sea still warm, the crowds gone, the light is Cézanne's light — Marseille at its best.
Foire aux Santons: Provence's clay nativity figures descend on the city in a two-century-old fair, with the scent of navettes alongside.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: Marseille's food is Mediterranean, direct, and shaped by the port. The ingredients come from the sea and from the communities that arrived through it.

local_word.definition: The aperitif of Marseille: anise-flavoured, diluted with cold water, which turns it cloudy. Ricard and Pernod are the brands; Marseillais have opinions about which. Served in a tall glass, with a small pitcher of cold water on the side. One part pastis to five parts water is the ratio — though the Marseillais pour generously. Every café terrace, every pétanque game, every Sunday lunch starts here.

items.name: Bouillabaisse — the original
items.description: Not a soup — a method. Specific rockfish (rascasse, grondin, Saint-Pierre, vive) simmered in saffron, fennel, and olive oil broth, then served in two courses: first the broth with rouille (garlic-saffron aioli) spread on grilled bread, then the fish separately. The Bouillabaisse Charter defines the required species. Made correctly, it takes hours and costs accordingly. The cheap versions are fish soup. This is architecture.
items.tag: Charter restaurants only · two courses · expensive and worth it

items.name: Panisse — Marseille street food
items.description: A thick chickpea flour cake, fried until crisp outside and soft inside, served in sticks or rounds. Originally brought by Genoese immigrants — Marseille absorbed it, made it its own. Found at the Marché de Noailles and at street stalls across the city. Hot, cheap, and better than it sounds. The version at L'Estaque with a cold beer is the correct order.

items.name: Rouille — the essential condiment
items.description: A thick, intensely orange emulsion of garlic, saffron, and olive oil — more forceful than aioli, less subtle than mayonnaise. Spread on the croutons that go into the bouillabaisse broth. Also eaten with grilled fish and fried vegetables. The colour comes from saffron and pepper; the heat comes from the garlic. Every Marseille restaurant makes its own. The quality varies significantly.
items.tag: With bouillabaisse · grilled fish · the best ones are orange-red

items.name: Navette — the biscuit of Saint-Victor
items.description: A dry, boat-shaped biscuit flavoured with orange blossom water, made since 1781 by the Four des Navettes bakery near the Abbaye Saint-Victor. The shape references the small boats said to have carried Mary Magdalene and the early Christians to Provence. Sold year-round at the bakery. Hard and dry — meant for dipping in coffee or pastis. Not a snack; a tradition.
items.tag: Four des Navettes · since 1781 · near Saint-Victor

items.name: Tapenade and anchoïade — Provençal basics
items.description: Tapenade: black olives, capers, anchovies, and olive oil blended to a paste — the name comes from the Provençal word for caper. Anchoïade: a rougher, more pungent paste of anchovies and garlic. Both spread on bread, served before meals, eaten at every terrace. Marseille sits at the edge of Provence; these are the flavours that have been here the longest.
items.tag: Every terrace · before meals · with bread and pastis

items.name: Café at the bar — the real Marseille rhythm
items.description: Stand at the bar. Order a petit café. Pay and leave within ten minutes. The terrace surcharge at Vieux-Port cafés adds a visible premium — locals know to stand at the zinc. Morning at the Noailles market, a coffee at a counter, watching the neighbourhood open: this is the most honest version of the city. It costs less than a euro and nothing else in Marseille will tell you more.

callout.label: Marché de Noailles — the city's real kitchen
callout.text: Noailles is where Marseille actually shops. The streets around Rue Longue-des-Capucins fill with stalls every morning: North African spices, fresh olives, merguez, Provençal herbs, preserved lemons, flatbreads from the oven. The smells are North Africa and Provence simultaneously. No tourist infrastructure, no English menus. Go hungry, bring cash, eat standing up. This is where the city feeds itself.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Marseille's famous for the port and the basilica. Both are worth it. But the city has a second layer that most visitors never reach.

items.name: Vallon des Auffes
items.description: A small cove cut into the Corniche, reached by walking under the viaduct that carries the coastal road above. A dozen colourful fishing boats, a cluster of houses built into the rock, two or three restaurants serving the catch of the day. The fishermen are still there — not for show. In summer, locals sit on the rocks at sunset with a bottle. Bus 83 passes directly above; look down from the bus window and you'll see why you get off. Free, always open.
items.rarity: A tiny fishing port hidden under a road bridge — 15 minutes from the Vieux-Port

items.name: L'Estaque
items.description: Ten kilometres north of the centre, on the edge of the bay. Cézanne came here repeatedly from 1870 to 1882; Braque, Dufy, and Derain followed. The bay and the factory chimneys appeared in dozens of works that became the foundation of Cubism. The village today has a small beach, a handful of fishermen's restaurants, and almost no visitors. Bus 35 from Joliette metro takes 25 minutes. The chichi frégi — fried dough sold from stands near the port — is the local snack. Go on a weekday.
items.rarity: A Cézanne and Braque village that no guidebook sends anyone to

items.name: La Vieille Charité — Le Panier
items.description: Built between 1671 and 1749 as a poorhouse, designed by Pierre Puget — Marseille's most important Baroque architect. Three floors of arcaded galleries around a courtyard, with a small domed chapel at the centre. Now houses the Museum of Mediterranean Archaeology and the Museum of African, Oceanic and Amerindian Arts. The architecture alone justifies the walk up through Le Panier. The courtyard is free to enter; museums are ticketed.
items.rarity: The 17th-century almshouse that became the city's most beautiful cultural space

items.name: La Friche la Belle de Mai
items.description: A 45,000 m² former SEITA tobacco factory in the Belle de Mai neighbourhood, 15 minutes by foot from the centre. Converted into a cultural complex: artist studios, performance halls, a cinema, exhibition spaces, shared gardens, and a rooftop terrace with panoramic views over the city. The rooftop bar is open in summer — drinks, city view, no tourist infrastructure. Not on the standard itinerary because it requires actually leaving the port area. Take bus 49 from Réformés-Canebière.
items.rarity: A former tobacco factory with a rooftop bar that the tourists haven't found

items.name: Cathédrale de la Major
items.description: One of the largest churches in France, built in the second half of the 19th century in striped Romanesque-Byzantine style — alternating green and white stone, golden mosaics inside, soaring domes. It sits directly next to MuCEM and most visitors walk past it to get to the museum. Free entry. The interior is dark, cool, and almost completely empty. The contrast with the crowds immediately outside is absolute.
items.rarity: The cathedral larger than Notre-Dame de Paris — that no one enters

items.name: Calanque de Sormiou
items.description: The closest calanque to the city and the most accessible — bus B1 from Castellane metro runs directly to the trailhead. A 30-minute walk down to a turquoise bay enclosed by white limestone cliffs. In summer, access by car is restricted; in spring and autumn, the path is nearly empty. There is a small seasonal restaurant at the bottom. The water is clear enough to see the bottom at five metres depth. Free. Check fire restrictions before going in summer.
items.rarity: The cove the Calanques tour boats skip

items.name: Cours Julien
items.description: 15 minutes' walk from the Vieux-Port. Street art, independent cafés, record shops, vintage stores, and one of the largest open-air street art areas in France. On Wednesday mornings, an organic farmers' market sets up on Place Jean Jaurès — around thirty local producers, fresh Provençal produce. In the evenings, the bars fill up with an entirely local crowd. Food at half the price of the Vieux-Port, twice the atmosphere. Free to walk, eat, sit.
items.rarity: The bohemian square where locals actually hang out

items.name: Palais Longchamp
items.description: Built in 1869 to celebrate the canal that finally brought water to the city — a palace constructed above a reservoir. At the centre, a grand waterfall and sculpture group; in the two wings, the Museum of Fine Arts and the Natural History Museum. Behind it, an expansive park: picnic lawns, playgrounds, shaded paths. Tram T2 to the Longchamp stop, 3-minute walk. Gardens and exterior always free; museums ticketed, free on the first Sunday of every month.
items.rarity: Two museums, spectacular gardens — almost no tourists

items.name: Notre-Dame de la Garde — La Bonne Mère
items.description: At 162 metres, the highest point in Marseille. A 30–40 minute uphill walk on the footpath, or bus 60 from Hôtel de Ville. From the top: the entire city, the Vieux-Port, the islands, and the open sea. Inside: hundreds of ex-votos — votive offerings left by sailors, mothers, survivors — covering the walls. The basilica itself is 19th-century Romanesque-Byzantine. Free entry. Go at dusk — the light at that hour is different.
items.rarity: 360 degrees over the city — worth the climb

callout.label: The Calanques — how to actually get there
callout.text: The standard advice is to take a boat tour from the Vieux-Port — the better option is to go yourself. Bus B1 from Castellane metro (line 1) runs to Luminy; from there, it's a 90-minute hike to Calanque de Sugiton, no facilities, bring everything. The same line goes to Sormiou — 30-minute walk down, a seasonal restaurant at the bottom, better for swimming. Both routes are free. Start before 09:00 in summer. The boat tours show you the cliffs from the outside; the trails put you inside them.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Go to the Vieux-Port fish market before 10:00
items.sub: Fishermen selling direct from boats. Daily, Quai des Belges. Free. Done by 10:00 — arrive at 08:00.

items.label: Walk the MuCEM terrace and Fort Saint-Jean
items.sub: MuCEM outdoor walkways and Fort Saint-Jean are free. Museum galleries are ticketed. First Sunday of the month: galleries also free.

items.label: Climb to Notre-Dame de la Garde (La Bonne Mère)
items.sub: Free entry. Bus 60 from Hôtel de Ville or 30–40 min walk uphill. Best at dusk. Views cover the entire city, the islands, and the Calanques.

items.label: Walk through Le Panier in the morning
items.sub: Free. Go before 11:00 before the day-trippers arrive. La Vieille Charité courtyard is free to enter — museums inside are ticketed.

items.label: Take bus 83 along the Corniche
items.sub: RTM ticket. Sit on the left. Look for Vallon des Auffes below the bridge — get off and walk down.

items.label: Eat bouillabaisse once, at a charter restaurant
items.sub: Expensive and worth it. Look for restaurants signed up to the Bouillabaisse Charter. Two courses. This is where the dish was invented.

items.label: Drink a pastis on a café terrace
items.sub: Anise aperitif, diluted with cold water. Ricard or Pernod. Order a carafe of water with it. Every café in the city.

items.label: Go to Marché de Noailles
items.sub: Free. Every morning, Rue Longue-des-Capucins. North African spices, olives, fresh produce. Bring cash. Eat standing up.

items.label: Hike to a calanque
items.sub: Free. Bus B1 from Castellane metro to Sormiou (30-min walk) or Luminy for Sugiton (90-min hike). Check fire restrictions online before going.

items.label: Find Vallon des Auffes
items.sub: Free. Walk from the Corniche under the viaduct. Fishing boats, rock-built houses, sunset on the water. Bus 83 stops above.

items.label: Enter the Cathédrale de la Major
items.sub: Free. Next to MuCEM. Striped stone exterior, golden mosaics inside, almost never crowded. Most visitors walk straight past it.

items.label: Visit L'Estaque on a weekday
items.sub: Bus 35 from Joliette, 25 minutes. The village where Cézanne and Braque painted. Small beach, fishermen's restaurants, no tourists. Try the chichi frégi.

checklist.title: Marseille Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Vous avez fait le vrai Marseille.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Marseille is a city without pretence; even its traps are obvious. Know these four and trust the city with the rest.

items.name: 'Bouillabaisse' under 40 euros
items.description: Real bouillabaisse demands at least four kinds of rockfish and two services; the orange soup on cheap menus is fish stock in costume.
items.instead: Go to one of the classics that signed the charter — Fonfon, Miramar; expensive, but eat the real thing once.

items.name: Photo menus on the Vieux-Port quay
items.description: The rows of harbour-view terraces sell the day's tired fish at tourist prices.
items.instead: Walk two streets inland, or drop into a small cove like Vallon des Auffes: same sea, honest kitchen.

items.name: Fake 'Savon de Marseille'
items.description: The colourful perfumed cubes in souvenir shops are often imported imitations; the real one bears the 72% oil stamp and comes from just four soap works.
items.instead: Look for the 72% stamp; buy from the historic soap factories' own shops or a trusted seller.

items.name: Going to the Calanques unprepared
items.description: In summer, road access closes and trails can shut for fire risk; the unprepared turn back under a punishing sun.
items.instead: Go early, carry water, check access the day before; or approach by boat from the sea — earn your first sight of Sormiou.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: In Marseille, beauty comes unpolished: the best cove has no sunbeds, the best bar no sign, the best fish no show. If you see polish, the price is a tourist price.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: The port, the Panier and the Good Mother's hill

steps.title: Vieux-Port fish market
steps.description: Watch fish go from boat to stall on the quay; the market ends at 10:00, come early.

steps.title: The lanes of Le Panier
steps.description: Get lost in the city's oldest quarter: street art, washing lines, the calm courtyard of the Vieille Charité.

steps.title: Lunch in Noailles
steps.description: Among the stalls of 'the belly of Marseille': panisse, kebab, North African aromas. The city's true seasoning.

steps.title: MuCEM + Cathédrale de la Major
steps.description: From the lace-concrete museum, stretch over the sea by footbridge; the striped cathedral is lovely while waiting for dusk.

steps.title: Notre-Dame de la Garde
steps.description: Climb the hill and watch city and sea from under La Bonne Mère: Marseille's best view, free.

steps.title: Evening on Cours Julien
steps.description: A bar on the graffiti-covered square, live music, pastis. The night stretches long here.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Port and hills
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: market, Panier, MuCEM, Bonne Mère.

steps.title: Calanques day
steps.description: Sormiou early in the morning, or the coves by boat; sea, trail and rest. Fish dinner at Vallon des Auffes on return.

steps.title: L'Estaque and art
steps.description: Panisse and chichi frégi in Cézanne's harbour L'Estaque, La Friche la Belle de Mai in the afternoon, farewell around Palais Longchamp at night.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: French opens doors; Marseille slang wins hearts. With these five you belong on the quay.

items.meaning: Hello — the mandatory first word of every exchange
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — pastis glasses rise to this
Marseille slang for 'nobody' — 'craint dégun': fears no one, the city's motto
